#4814. What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

The AI tool reportedly used to breach a system shared by three U.S. intelligence agencies is already part of the arsenal of at least six hacking groups tracked by Microsoft, according to research published Wednesday.

Artex, a framework originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals find security flaws, was reportedly involved in an intrusion affecting the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The compromised system analyzes information collected from publicly available sources, according to the Associated Press. The identity of the hackers and the AI model they used remain unconfirmed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In one analysis, Microsoft's threat intelligence team identified both financially motivated criminals and state-sponsored groups using the software, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Storm-0940, and Storm-3358. Microsoft did not attribute the spy agency breach to any of them.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

The CIA intrusion, disclosed Tuesday, affected a shared intelligence analysis system that draws on sources such as social media, commercial satellite imagery, and data brokers. A source told Nextgov/FCW that the breach had been resolved and classified systems were unaffected. What information, if any, was stolen remains unclear, though such an intrusion could expose analysts' investigative priorities.

The NSA suffered a similar breach exposing unclassified information, according to the New York Times. Prior, the NSA's classified internal communications network was restored on November 20 after several days of disruption. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the outage to software patching rather than a cyberattack. The Donald Trump administration has denied that the recent outages were part of a coordinated attack.

Separately, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide that contains criminal histories, records of missing persons, fugitives, and stolen property. Investigators have not publicly established the extent of the intrusion or whether records were stolen.

Artex is not an AI model like ChatGPT's GPT or Anthropic's Claude. It is an agentic harness, a piece of software that lets language models interact with other programs and perform tasks rather than simply generate text.

A developer known as Autumn-27 published the project on GitHub in July. Written in Go, it was designed for penetration testing, the practice of attempting to break into computer systems with the owner's permission to identify security weaknesses.

The framework divides work among specialized AI agents responsible for planning, carrying out assessments, and reporting their results, according to Google's threat intelligence team. A shared record of findings helps the agents retain context and coordinate their work over lengthy assignments.

The underlying AI is interchangeable. Microsoft says Artex can use commercial and open-weight models, which means the framework is not necessarily subject to the safety policies of any one AI company.

Microsoft says that under certain conditions Artex can obtain lasting access with elevated permissions in minutes, rather than requiring someone to oversee each stage of an operation.

Artex attracted international attention in October after attacks on South Korean financial institutions. A November 13 FBI advisory linked the campaign to the theft of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Autumn-27 removed the original repository in October following reports of criminal abuse. By early November, researchers had counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed Artex installations, according to the FBI, though that does not mean all were operated by criminals.

Removing an open-source repository does not erase the copies others have downloaded or the independent versions they have created. Microsoft says that this month Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of Artex and began selling access to a commercial offering called Artex Pro.

The problem is not unique to Artex. Security researchers have long released tools that criminals later repurposed, but AI reduces the amount of manual work involved in running them.

The FBI has tracked Artex-related activity across 10 industries since August, including government, defense, finance, and technology.

On November 13, Amazon researchers described campaigns believed to involve Artex, including attempts to steal AI service credentials and circumvent identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

The identity verification system rejected every synthetic video attempt documented by the agents. Amazon also cautioned that it could not independently verify all the outcomes the agents claimed to have achieved.

As Decrypt reported last year, Anthropic said suspected Chinese state-sponsored hackers had already used Claude to automate 80% to 90% of the tactical work in a cyberespionage campaign targeting roughly 30 organizations.

Smaller criminal groups now have access to software that handles some of the coordination previously left to experienced hackers. They still need vulnerable targets, and defenders can still stop them.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said Tuesday that it had seen a sharp increase in AI-assisted attacks since September, with criminals exploiting familiar problems such as poorly secured accounts and misconfigured software.

For organizations defending themselves, the immediate priority remains fixing those weaknesses, reducing the number of publicly exposed systems, and improving detection. Britain's cybersecurity agency says today's agentic frameworks are relatively noisy, giving defenders a chance to spot them, though future versions may be harder to detect.

#4813. Solana DEX Velocity halts trading over bug just months after relaunch

Velocity relaunched in September as a rebuilt version of Drift Protocol, which was attacked by North Korean hackers in April.

Solana-based decentralized exchange Velocity said Wednesday it has suspended all transactions while its team works to fix a bug.

“User deposits are safe,” Velocity said in a post on X, and that the protocol would remain paused until it was safe to resume.

Velocity is the rebuilt, forked version of Drift Protocol, which was hacked in April. Velocity relaunched under the new name in September.

Unlike Drift Protocol, Velocity DEX focuses exclusively on perpetual futures trading, removing standalone spot trading. Data from DefiLlama shows its perp volume saw a significant spike in November, with the biggest spike in volume on Nov. 18 and 19.

Velocity said it will share more about the bug on social media.

Drift reported about $295 million in losses from an April 1 hack, which has been blamed on UNC6862, a North Korean threat group.

#4809. South Korea’s crypto bill could move stablecoin race beyond token issuance

South Korea’s draft bill favors bank-led stablecoin issuance but allows fintech and technology companies to become the largest individual shareholders.

South Korean fintech companies could gain influence in bank-led stablecoin groups by signing up partners that help people spend won-denominated tokens, Tiger Research said in its Tuesday report.

“Those relationships are likely to matter more to the business than the volume of stablecoins issued,” the Asia-focused research company said.

On Tuesday, South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) unveiled its draft digital assets bill that would initially limit issuance of won-denominated stablecoins to consortiums in which banks collectively hold a majority stake. A fintech or technology company could still hold a larger stake than any individual bank.

The proposal follows months of regulatory disagreements. The Bank of Korea has advocated for bank-led issuance, citing monetary policy and financial stability risks, while the FSC previously favored allowing nonbank companies to issue stablecoins.

If the Banking Act’s 15% limit on a bank’s stake in a nonfinancial company applies to stablecoin issuers, at least four banks would need to join each consortium to secure a majority, according to Tiger Research.

Vincent Chok, founder and CEO of First Digital, whose subsidiary issues the FDUSD stablecoin, told Cointelegraph that bank-majority consortiums could give won-denominated stablecoins credibility at launch, while fintech participation could help preserve innovation.

“Beyond who issues, Korea’s ability to capture the wider economic activity around stablecoins will rest on efficient on- and off-ramps and rails connecting KRW with global dollar liquidity,” Chok said.

South Korean financial and technology companies have already started exploring these opportunities. In May, KB Financial Group completed a won-denominated stablecoin pilot covering merchant payments and cross-border remittances. In July, Viva Republica, which operates the Toss payments app, partnered with Optimism and Sunnyside Labs to test stablecoin-based payments for financial institutions.

Related: How South Korea’s proposed 20% cap could change who runs Upbit

The bill still needs to pass the National Assembly before proceeding to presidential promulgation. Tiger Research said the legislation is expected to take effect one year after promulgation, while key details, including shareholder requirements for stablecoin consortiums, remain subject to subsequent enforcement decrees.

#4804. Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

For the second time in weeks, a major Bitcoin mining firm has warned that attackers are siphoning mining rewards by hijacking the internet connections between miners and their pools, a sign that a long-dormant weakness in mining’s plumbing is now being exploited at scale.

Mining software firm Braiins said Wednesday that an attacker struck more than a thousand mining sites in a single second on Nov. 20, rerouting their connections to an impostor pool.

It follows a similar incident just last week, when mining-services firm Luxor reported that hackers had redirected miner rewards, which it tied to AI-assisted attacks.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The two firms described somewhat different mechanisms, but the effect was the same: hashrate quietly diverted away from the miners who produced it.

In its security alert, Braiins stressed the attacker didn’t need to break into any miner or into Braiins Pool itself. Instead, they exploited a long-standing flaw in Stratum V1, the unencrypted, plain-text protocol that carries work between miners and pools and offers no way to verify that the server on the other end is the real pool.

By rerouting traffic, the attacker impersonated the pool, fed miners legitimate-looking jobs, and pocketed the resulting shares under their own account at a separate pool.

The scheme hinged on manipulating the Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, the trust-based system that tells networks where to route internet traffic. The attacker announced a narrower, more specific block of addresses that included a pool’s Stratum endpoint, causing networks that failed to validate the route to funnel miners’ connections to the impostor.

Hijacked machines kept hashing at full power while their pool dashboards showed zero hashrate, making the theft nearly invisible on-site.

Braiins traced episodes starting in early November across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Argentina, before a larger Nov. 20 wave hit mostly European miners, diverting between 0.6 and 1.9 exahashes per second at a time. The firm characterized the short, escalating bursts as the attacker “testing the waters,” noting the diverted hashrate grew more than tenfold in two weeks.

The technique isn’t new. Braiins noted that Dell SecureWorks documented the same routing trick stealing roughly $83,000 in mining rewards back in 2014, and the firm has warned about “hashrate hijacking” since 2020 as a reason to adopt the encrypted Stratum V2 protocol.

For years, the industry treated it as rare enough to tolerate; now, two firms in a matter of weeks have flagged it hitting miners in the wild.

Braiins urged the whole industry to act, recommending miners move to Stratum V2 or Stratum V1 over TLS with certificate verification, strip out plain-text backup connections, and push network operators to validate routes. It also released a free proxy tool for miners that can’t upgrade.

Any miner still on plain Stratum V1, the firm said, “is a target, on any pool.”

#4801. Stablecoin redemptions hit $12B in 30 days, echoing 2022 bear market

Crypto research firm Kaiko said the cash-out was smaller than in 2022 and has slowed, with stablecoin supply down just 0.4% since Nov. 13.

Net redemptions across the 11 stablecoins tracked by crypto research firm Kaiko reached about $12 billion in the 30 days to Nov. 13, echoing a pattern analysts saw during the 2022 bear market.

Tether’s USDt (USDT) and Circle’s USDC (USDC), the two largest stablecoins, each ended the period with about 4% fewer tokens in circulation. Since Nov. 13, total stablecoin supply has fallen just 0.4%, while USDC supply has edged higher.

“The contraction looks like capital leaving crypto rather than rotating within it,” Kaiko analyst Andrew Yang told Cointelegraph.

Yang said that the redemptions left traders with fewer stablecoins on hand to buy crypto.

The cash-out coincided with outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and a shift in expectations toward tighter Federal Reserve policy.

Daily trading volume in USDT pairs was about half its 2025 average over the past month, according to Kaiko. Bitcoin (BTC) market makers continued to post orders close to the market price.

The dollar value of orders to buy or sell Bitcoin within 1% of its market price fell about 15% over the past month. Measured in Bitcoin, those orders were 9% larger in aggregate, Yang said.

Related: Stablecoin supply falls $14.2B in biggest 30-day drop since June 2022

Nearly 90% of the 30-day decline in stablecoin supply came from Ethereum, a major hub for exchanges and decentralized finance. On Tron, a network more commonly used for payments, stablecoin supply fell just 1.4%, according to Kaiko.

Onchain transfers of USDT and USDC have averaged about $157 billion a day so far this quarter. That’s above the 2025 daily average of $130 billion, though below the pace in the fourth quarter of last year, Kaiko said.

During the 2022–2023 bear market, rising interest rates and falling crypto prices drove months of redemptions from fiat-backed stablecoins, Yang said. He described the current pullback as much smaller and pointed to a more recent comparison. Stablecoin supply fell from mid-May into June this year before stabilizing in August.

For USDT, the latest decline is the largest since 2022, said Julio Moreno, head of research at blockchain analytics firm CryptoQuant. Its market capitalization has fallen $9 billion over the past 60 days, a drop Moreno linked to a broader retreat from risk assets, including stocks and commodities.

Moreno tracks USDT supply as a measure of the funds available for trading. Exchanges hold 51% of the USDT circulating on Ethereum, he told Cointelegraph.

USDT supply was also shrinking when Bitcoin bottomed in November 2022, Moreno said.

He said stablecoin supply would have to grow again “in order for liquidity to improve and the market to recover.”

#4798. French Senate rejects 100K euro crypto wallet disclosure requirement

Senators also rejected stablecoin-swap and crypto exit-tax proposals, while the 2027 budget remains under parliamentary consideration.

The French Senate rejected proposals Tuesday that would have required taxpayers to declare self-custodied crypto holdings worth at least 100,000 euros (about $109,600) to tax authorities.

Senators voted down identical amendments from Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny during debate on the 2027 budget. The requirement would have applied when the combined value of crypto held in wallets outside a service provider reached at least 100,000 euros on Dec. 31.

The reporting requirement was initially adopted by the National Assembly on Nov. 3, but fell when lawmakers rejected the budget’s entire revenue section on Nov. 4.

Budget Minister David Amiel opposed the wallet-reporting amendments, saying they would not enable authorities to track how crypto is used, particularly in money laundering or tax fraud. The Senate’s finance committee followed the government’s recommendation to reject them.

Requiring a declaration of wallet holdings without a taxable event would amount to “placing a blanket suspicion on good-faith users,” Faustine Fleuret, global head of public affairs at lending protocol Morpho, told Cointelegraph.

She said that self-custodial wallet reporting would create “unequal treatment” compared to other assets like jewelry or fine art, “whose mere holding is not subject to a reporting obligation in the absence of a taxable transaction.”

Related: Lagarde warns Europe could miss chance to unify tokenized markets

The Senate also rejected another amendment from Savoldelli that would have taxed gains on crypto conversions into stablecoins classified as electronic-money tokens under EU rules. It would have applied from Jan. 1, 2027.

The Assembly adopted a similar amendment from MP Nicolas Sansu on Oct. 16, but that measure also fell when the Assembly rejected the revenue section. Savoldelli reintroduced the proposal on Nov. 19 before Tuesday’s rejection.

A proposal to extend France’s exit tax to unrealized crypto gains when qualifying taxpayers moved their tax residence abroad also failed. The Assembly rejected similar proposals on Oct. 30.

Another crypto-related amendment remains pending. Senator Thomas Dossus’s amendment would raise a proposed fine for refusing tax authorities’ information requests from 10,000 euros to 50,000 euros per request. It would cover financial institutions, crypto service providers and platform operators.

The Senate is scheduled to complete debate and vote on the budget’s revenue section Saturday, with Sunday available if needed.

A Senate vote on the full budget is scheduled for Dec. 9. The rejected crypto measures are absent from the text as it stands, but the budget still faces further negotiations before final adoption.

#4797. The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

Password manager 1Password has disclosed a security breach in which an attacker accessed some of its backend systems and copied customer account information, though the company says the vaults where users store their passwords and other secrets were never touched.

In a disclosure published Tuesday, the Toronto-based firm said it began investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The intruder used that access to reach

1Password’s source code and push malicious code to backend services, which then downloaded administrative data on a subset of customers. At no point, the company said, were vault contents accessible to the attacker.

Here’s what was taken, according to 1Password: customer names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys (which are public by design), certain protocol parameters that can’t be used to access an account, and non-secret internal metadata.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the company’s software build systems, which hold some infrastructure credentials. 1Password said it has rotated all credentials that may have been exposed.

Crucially for users, the breach did not expose the data that actually matters: your vaults, the items inside them, the keys that protect them, or your account recovery keys.

1Password’s design means it never stores your account password or Secret Key, so an attacker who gets into its servers still can’t decrypt your vault. The company stressed there’s nothing you need to change in your account, and its apps and browser extensions are working normally.

What users should do, for now, comes down to what is generally good advice at all times: watch out for phishing emails, because they’re surely coming.

Because names and email addresses were exposed, affected users are prime targets for scam emails impersonating 1Password, particularly fake account-recovery or invitation requests.

The company urged caution with any unexpected message mentioning 1Password, and reiterated that it will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key, which you should only ever enter in the official app or on the official site after opening it yourself.

One wrinkle involves emailed invitation and recovery links, which contain a token. 1Password said a small number of users in that state were notified directly; as a precaution, it lengthened the verification codes in those emails from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters to make guessing them impractical.

The incident echoes a run of breaches hitting companies that hold users’ most sensitive data, a pattern that has emerged this year as attackers increasingly target third-party systems and developer accounts rather than the encryption itself.

#4795. HYPE drops 8% as Trump bump gives way to 40% slide from peak

HYPE traded below its price before Trump’s August remarks as wallets linked to Abraxas Capital reportedly exited the Hyperliquid platform.

Hyperliquid’s native token HYPE fell nearly 8% on Wednesday, trading below its price before US President Donald Trump’s remarks on US access to the exchange.

CoinGecko data showed HYPE (HYPE) at $58.14, about 40% below its Sept. 23 all-time high of $97.96. The token traded around $62 immediately before Trump’s remarks.

On Aug. 19, Trump said that Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig was working to bring Hyperliquid into the US. On Oct. 29, HYPE surged toward its record high after Intercontinental Exchange, owner of the NYSE, said it would seek approval for regulated Hyperliquid-based perpetual futures aimed at US retail traders.

Hyperliquid is a decentralized trading platform and layer-1 blockchain best known for its onchain perpetual futures exchange.

HYPE rallied from early-2026 lows near $20 to its September record as Hyperliquid expanded into markets beyond crypto. Its HIP-3 upgrade, live since October 2025, lets those who meet staking requirements deploy perpetual markets for a wide range of assets.

Related: Hong Kong adds Hyperliquid to list of ‘suspicious’ crypto platforms

Meanwhile, blockchain analytics account Lookonchain reported that wallets labeled by Arkham as belonging to Abraxas Capital exited Hyperliquid.

Lookonchain said the wallets sold 219,081 HYPE (about $13.25 million) and then bought 4,230 ETH ($7.09 million).

Cointelegraph reached out to Abraxas Capital to confirm the wallet attribution and reported exit but did not receive a response before publication.

Abraxas Capital Management was founded in 2002 and has specialized in digital assets since 2017. The London-based company is regulated by the UK Financial Conduct Authority.

Stablecoin giant Tether is a major investor in Abraxas’ flagship Elysium fund, according to court filings made public in July. Abraxas co-founder Fabio Frontini testified that Tether’s stake reached about $800 million, roughly 75% of the fund’s assets at the time.

#4794. Want Headphones Built for Real Workouts? These 9 Survived Runs, Jumps, and Gym-Bag Chaos

Headphones that can handle as much as you can.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Listening to a hyped-up playlist can make all the difference in your workout. As a fitness writer and longtime distance runner, I’ve seen firsthand how the right headphones can make or break a workout. And I’ve worked my way through a range of workout headphones before I found the ones I don’t want to be without.

I used to constantly fiddle with headphones that didn’t fit right, which is a real motivational buzzkill, and once spent 10 minutes trying to hunt down an earbud that popped out mid-run. (I never recovered it.) I’ve also discovered that some headphones are better for certain types of workouts over others. Case in point: My go-to headphones for strength training at the noisy gym are different from what I reach for when it comes to HIIT and running.

No matter the style and fit you prefer, elements like sweat resistance, battery life, sound quality, and adjustability are crucial, too. And, while I love a good bargain, I’ve learned that you can’t just grab any random pair of cheap headphones or earbuds and expect them to do the job well. After multiple rounds of testing, these are the best wireless workout headphones to consider.

The Apple AirPods Pro have always been a reliable pair of headphones for me, and the latest third generation is even better. Whether I’m biking or struggling through heavy reps, it delivers a premium experience, including impressive sound and a comfortable fit. And the latest edition further proves their God-tier status: heart rate, step, and calorie tracking.

It has a sensor that deciphers your pulse through your ear canals, which then calculates calories burned based on heart rate. I like to keep tabs on my heart rate during high-intensity cardio, so it’s a great alternative to wearing a fitness tracker. Just make sure the fit is right to get an accurate reading (four silicone ear cup sizes are available).

It also has motion sensors that can track your steps. All data transfers to the Apple Health app, so you need to own an iPhone or iPad. Luckily, I recently converted (sorry, Android).

When I’m grinding hard at the gym, I want to hear nothing around me except my hype house music. The active noise cancellation drowns out any grunters, loud gym music, TVs, and general unnecessary background noise. I feel like it’s just me and my music, so that I can laser-focus on the task at hand.

But when I need to maintain awareness during outdoor runs, I turn on transparency mode to hear oncoming traffic and people nearby. I also like that it automatically lowers my music when it detects me talking to someone. It has an IP57 rating, meaning it’s sweat and dust-resistant, and can be submerged in a meter of water for up to 30 minutes in case of any accidental puddle drops (been there). As someone who sweats a lot, each bud repels moisture very well and doesn’t fall out of my ears when jumping or running. Plus, sweat never clogs my ears—something I experienced with regular AirPods. Battery life could be better for all-day wear, but it’s good for workouts (assuming you’re not working out all day). I hit the gym after work, and the power is always drained after an eight-hour day. On the flip side, it’s easy to juice up in 15 minutes with the charging case (it offers up to 30 hours of battery life per charge). To fully restore the battery, make sure to charge overnight. Read More: Best Fitness Trackers

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are an absolute treasure. I own a lot of headphones, but the sound quality always keeps me coming back for more. The over-ear design completely covers my ears, providing A-grade noise cancellation at prime-time hours.

The sound is immersive with balanced, deep bass that doesn’t feel piercing—an issue with lower-quality headphones I tested. I blast my tunes at full volume when getting in the zone, and I never feel uncomfortable.

They look bulky, but looks can be deceiving. They never budge, even when speed walking at an incline or doing fast-paced plyometric drills. I’ve worn it during box jumps and ice skaters, and it stayed put.

Just note it’s not water resistant for intense cardio like spinning and running, where you’ll work up a sweat—although the plush padding rimming the headband and ear cups can easily be wiped clean.

Like the Apple AirPods Pro 3, I have to charge it daily in the included case, so make sure to keep the cable on hand for quick power-ups.

Read More: The Best Slim Fitness Trackers

If you really just can’t with the possibility of your earbuds falling out, but still want a compact option, Dr. Dre delivered just what you need: the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. It has hooks that seamlessly glide over the ears, ensuring a proper fit that stays put. And compared to the previous iteration that launched six years ago, it’s now smaller and lighter, and shares many of the same features as the AirPods Pro 3 (Apple does own Beats, after all), including active noise cancellation, transparency mode, and heart rate monitoring through the Beats app.

I’ve put it to the test during long runs, sprints, low-impact biking, and strength training. The verdict? It performs as sleekly as it looks. The sound is crisp and rich, while the bass is heavy without being overbearing.The sweat resistance is a notch below AirPods with an IPX4 rating, meaning it can withstand light rain but can’t be submerged. I’ve gotten caught in the rain one too many times while wearing these—yet, the sound quality is still the same as it was straight out of the box. And battery life is actually slightly better than AirPods, offering up to 45 hours with the charging case.However, this pair feels more uncomfortable than the Apple AirPods Pro 3. The material feels a little too hard for my liking. If you plan on walking or running for hours, the best overall is the way to go.

The last thing you want is uncomfortable headphones when in the midst of PRing your next barbell squat. Working out is tough enough, so having a pair that’s übersoft will take away some of the pain. Meet the Sony WH-1000XM6—a splurge that’s worth the investment.

Thick foam on the ear cups feels like lying on a pillow, while it also seals sound better for superior noise cancellation. The wide headband is plush and fits securely onto the head without being too tight. MH senior gear and commerce editor Ryan Brower throws it in his gym bag whenever he has strength training on deck. He also appreciates the adjustable smooth slider for a custom fit, calling it a fluid mechanism.

The headphones use 12 microphones to isolate and cancel out sound to deliver an immersive listening experience. Vocals and instruments sound balanced and rich, with Brower calling the sound quality superb. Battery life can run for up to 30 hours, while just three minutes of charging can provide three hours—perfect if you’re in a rush to hit the gym.

Brower’s only gripes are the lack of sweat resistance for high-intensity activities, like running or spinning, and that it feels a little bulky. So, he reserves it for less strenuous pursuits.

If you’re into an over-ear design in headphones, you know they can get hot and sweaty fast. But the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones feel surprisingly breathable on—for an over-ear headphone. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

These headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can quickly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

The Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A big draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

The earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an issue with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

Some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

These earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

The earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

If you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

The strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

The silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

The sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an issue since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

If blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I quickly need it before a run.

Full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” says Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

Having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

For example, the total playtime for the new Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

You have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this issue. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

As a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

#4793. Mauviel's Copper Cookware Is 25% Off For Black Friday

There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few. As seen in this Sag Harbor home, this Parisian pied-à-terre, this Westchester residence, and this Connecticut country retreat, Mauviel is something of a status symbol in kitchens. Much like a Le Creuset Dutch oven out on display, spying a few copper pans from the French brand hanging from a rail signals that “Great Taste Lives Here.” And this week marks a good opportunity to join the club, with Mauviel sets and individual pieces up to 30% off for Black Friday at Williams Sonoma and on Shop.

I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast. Of course it does. Unlike some of my ceramic pans that catch and dry out an egg, the Mauviel has given me no trouble, delivering me the most perfect eggs to date I’ve ever cooked. Even against my stainless-steel pans (which I do love very much), these heat a bit more quickly and evenly.

That excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple. Mauviel has made copper cookware since 1830 in Villedieu-les-Poêles, a town in Normandy with an enduring history of copper manufacturing; the pieces are still handcrafted there. As far as their makeup, the M’150 B pieces are, for example, 1.5 millimeters thick and constructed of a 90% polished copper exterior and a 10% stainless-steel interior. They heat evenly; are immediately responsive to heat adjustments; and work on gas, electric, and ceramic cooktops.

The pans partners with a copper kettle on the stove in this Portland manse by Jessica Helgerson.

The copper treasures do, however, require care. They’re not nonstick pots and pans, so you need a little oil or butter to get any slip. They’re hand-wash only, and Mauviel advises against using them for long stretches on high heat or leaving them empty on a hot burner. I don’t polish mine, simply because I don’t own any copper polish. The wear shows quickly, and I like that, though if AD were shooting my house, maybe I’d like it less.

The Black Friday markdowns run across the line: my copper fry pan is going for $280 in the 10-inch size (25% off), a 2.5-quart sauce pan is $450 (29% off), and a 15-piece cookware set is $3,000 (32% off). For anyone who cooks every day, it’s a hard gift to beat. I, for one, now can’t imagine frying my eggs any other way.

#4792. Bitcoin price may fall below $53K if bear-market history repeats

Bitcoin price downside targets focused on the $53,200 realized price as research saw pointed to bear-market patterns continuing for BTC/USD.

Bitcoin (BTC) is approaching investors’ aggregate cost basis, with previous bear markets pointing to the risk of further price declines.

New research from onchain analytics platform Glassnode shows BTC/USD now trades just 10% above its realized price.

Realized price represents the average price at which each Bitcoin last moved onchain. When the spot price falls below this level, currently around $53,200, holders are collectively sitting on an unrealized loss.

BTC/USD one-week chart with realized price. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

During prior bear markets, Bitcoin fell through its realized price before establishing its next long-term floor.

“In each of those bear markets, however, price ended up well below the Realized Price,” Glassnode wrote in the latest edition of its The Week Onchain newsletter.

During Bitcoin’s last bear market in 2022, price spent 180 days below realized price before reclaiming it in January 2023. The record for time spent below investors’ aggregate cost basis is 301 days across 2014 and 2015, per calculations from Bitfinex Alpha, the research arm of crypto exchange Bitfinex.

Applying previous declines below realized price to today’s level would put Bitcoin at about $45,000 in a repeat of the March 2020 crash, or around $41,000 and $37,000 using the 2022 and 2018 bear-market lows, respectively.

“Should this time not be different after all, we would expect price to go lower and close below the Realized Price, which is a little over 10% away,” Glassnode added.

Bitcoin realized price comparison. Source: Glassnode

Both older and younger investor cohorts continue to realize losses onchain following Bitcoin’s fall Saturday to its lowest level since September 2024.

Related: Bitcoin slides amid US tariff nerves as Anthropic falls below IPO price

Glassnode noted that relative to capital inflows, aggregate onchain losses now run at their highest level since the end of the 2022 bear market during the implosion of crypto exchange FTX — a sign that “capitulation has begun.”

“In the past, spikes like this often came close to the lows, as in early 2019, March 2020 and November 2022. They can also come early, as in February 2018 and in May and June 2022, with lower prices still ahead,” it continued.

Bitcoin onchain loss data. Source: Glassnode

#4791. What Happened to Alice Huang, the Woman at the Center of Nvidia’s Scandal?

What Happened to Alice Huang, the Woman at the Center of Nvidia’s Scandal?

While Jensen Huang has returned to the helm of Nvidia following a brief but dramatic departure, the Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal that threatened his career remains largely out of public view.

U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers on Tuesday that they had found no evidence that Alice Huang was instructed by Chinese intelligence to spy on the Nvidia chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the classified briefing.

Although officials claimed that she had contacted China's intelligence service during the affair, they found no indication that she had passed on significant intelligence. The assessment could change if new evidence emerges.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The findings mark a significant development in a controversy that has shaken Silicon Valley—and the whole global economy alongside it—and heightened tensions over China's access to advanced American technology.

But for Alice Huang, questions surrounding her business activities, legal situation and future remain unresolved.

Also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le, Alice Huang is a Hong Kong resident who previously led Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing company that became a major customer of Nvidia.

The company originated as the overseas subsidiary of a Chinese video game business before shifting into artificial intelligence infrastructure. It became an official Nvidia cloud partner in November 2023.

According to corporate records cited by the Associated Press, Huang ceased to be a registered director of Megaspeed in November 2023, although Singaporean authorities identified her as its chief executive, chairperson and a key controller when they investigated the company in 2025.

Megaspeed said on November 15 that Huang had formally departed on August 30, 2025, and no longer held any position within the company. It declined to discuss her private affairs and maintained that its business operations were lawful.

Huang's troubles with Singaporean authorities began well before the allegations of espionage became public.

Singapore launched an investigation in February 2025 into suspected false declarations involving purchases of computer servers and their eventual destinations.

Police questioned Huang in June that year and retained her passport to ensure her availability during the investigation.

In February 2026, authorities determined that there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed offences related to the suspected false declarations.

However, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said investigators believed Huang had knowingly supplied inaccurate information to minimize her involvement in Megaspeed.

She received a formal warning and was prohibited from returning to Singapore. Authorities returned her passport on February 26, and she left the country that day.

Taiwanese authorities have also revoked her entry permit.

Speaking in Australia on Tuesday, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong reiterated that authorities had found no grounds to pursue prosecution against Huang, although investigations into Megaspeed were continuing.

Singapore has explicitly stated that its investigation of Huang did not concern espionage.

Bloomberg reported on November 12, citing anonymous sources, that Huang was in Beijing and that Chinese security officials were aware of her presence there. Her current whereabouts have not been independently confirmed.

Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations, while Huang herself has remained publicly silent in recent reporting.

Meanwhile, scrutiny of her business network continues to intensify.

On Wednesday, Reuters reported that companies connected to Huang's relatives and business associates had secured financing against AI servers and computing modules valued at $270 million in China.

The financial records did not establish whether the equipment contained chips subject to US export restrictions. Huang could not be reached for comment by Reuters.

The revelations followed Washington's decision on Monday to add Megaspeed and several related businesses to its trade blacklist.

While the latest intelligence assessment weakens the allegation that Huang was engaged in a Beijing-directed espionage operation, it does not settle the separate questions surrounding her commercial connections.

For now, Jensen Huang has reclaimed his position at one of the world's most influential technology companies. Alice Huang's professional future, however, remains uncertain.

#4789. The Best Matching Sweat Sets, Tested by Style and Fitness Editors

Just in time for Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Back in the day, a sweatsuit was all about comfort. It wasn’t so much a fashion staple, but the kind of thing to throw on and lounge in. With Y2K style back in vogue, matching sweatsuits are more commonplace than ever—just with a little less sparkle than the ones previously sported by icons like Paris Hilton and J.Lo in the early 2000s. And, with the rise of athleisure, these simple sweats have gotten the luxury treatment: they’re softer, more flattering, and pricier than ever.

Whether you’re the kind of person who considers it a cozy wardrobe essential, or you’re just looking to treat yourself to something comfortable to wear around the house, there have never been more choices when it comes to the best matching sweatsuits. Since we’re heading into winter (and Black Friday is just around the corner!), Women’s Health editors tested the most popular styles.

Here are our thoughts on the matching sets after months of lounging in them, working from home in them, and even wearing them to work.

Oner Active’s workout clothes have had our hearts at WH for a while. That’s why we were excited to put their loungewear to the test. Associate Health and Fitness editor Addison Aloian wore this set while traveling, chilling at home, and even working behind the scenes on a photoshoot.

“I absolutely love this set from Oner,” she says. She loves it for its comfort, warmth, and versatility (Aloian says she knows she could wear it outside in the chilly NYC winter, layer it under her ski clothes, or pop it on over leggings for her warm-up at the gym). “But the standout feature is the color,” Aloian says. “So many sweat sets are gray or black, but the turquoise is stunning and makes it a standout in my closet when I want a monochromatic moment.” She opted for the “oil blue” color, but Oner also has options like alpine green and toasted red, plus your neutral staples.

It’s also one of the more affordable options we tested—and on sale for half off this Black Friday. But that doesn’t mean it skimps on quality: The material feels super plush since it’s made from 67% cotton and 33% polyester, for a super plush feel that doesn’t pill or shed after one wash.

The set’s one flaw? The bottoms are a little long. At 5 '1, Aloian says she’d love a “short” option as well. Oner does offer a “long” length, though, for the taller girlies.

Old Navy Bounce Fleece Half-Zip Pullover Sweatshirt

Old Navy High-Waisted Bounce Fleece Jogger Sweatpants

In a world of expensive sweat sets, Old Navy’s Bounce Fleece line provides a budget-friendly—and stylish—option. “You’d never know these are super affordable,” says Fitness editor Cori Ritchey. They hold their own with the rest of the pricier sets from their fit to their feel.

The highlight for Ritchey is the material, a mix of polyester, rayon, and spandex. “It moves with you, and the fabric feels like it breathes compared to other sweatsuits that feel too heavy and hot.” One small caveat: Be sure to follow the wash instructions and keep your cycle on cold and gentle, tumble dry low, and keep the garments inside out. Ritchey says she noticed a bit of pilling after the first wash, but says that after following the wash instructions during the next few washes, the set stayed in great shape.

The half-zip and jogger combo makes for a put-together look and is cozy enough for traveling, running errands, or lounging around the house, Ritchey says. The set comes in plenty of neutral colors, plus some fun ones like orchid. It’s also the first on our list that doesn’t have a prominent logo, for anyone who wants a clean-looking set with no branding. Another point for Old Navy: It’s the most size-inclusive on the list. Sizing goes from XS to 4XL, with regular, tall, and petite options.

Alo is another longtime favorite at WH. The brand is known for its cozy, stylish (and premium-priced) loungewear. The fit is what we love most. The set, which comes in over a dozen colors, has an oversized feel, yet still manages to look intentional, says Deputy Features editor Carina Hsieh. “Unlike other sweatsuits, this one doesn’t look or feel unflattering or sloppy,” she says. It’s also the “perfect transition-weather sweatsuit.” The French terry material is made up of 65% cotton and 35% polyester, for a “really soft, thick, and high-quality” feel. The fabric doesn’t feel ultra-heavy, though, so it’s a great pick for fall and spring when you might overheat in thicker sets. Another perk? The pants have pockets.

However, the sizing isn’t the most intuitive. Hsieh, who is typically a small or medium in other brands, is an extra-extra small in these pants. The pants also run a bit long. Hsieh says sizing down is likely the way to go for this set.

Aritzia Cozy Sweatfleece Mega Funnel Neck

I had been hearing great things about Aritzia’s Sweatfleece line, and after testing for over a month, I can attest that it’s truly the coziest sweat set I’ve worn. Made from 78% cotton and 22% polyester, the material is soft with a fleece-lined interior. They’ll definitely keep you warm; that fleece inside is perfect for chilly temps. But they don’t feel too heavy. The material is still breathable, and I don’t get overheated when I’m wearing them.

I also love the look of this set, especially with the funnel/mockneck style—which is very on-trend. I have been wearing the suit when I work from home, and it makes me feel put together and chic, even though I’m in the coziest clothes I own. I’m also a runner, and I've noticed that this is the first thing I want to put on after I shower post-run. It’s the ultimate comfy outfit for recovery.

When it comes to sizing, these sweats have a “mega” fit, which means they’re oversized. I still sized up just to make sure mine would be roomy, but learned that I didn’t need to. These give you an oversized fit at your true size. Plus, as a shorter girlie (5’2!), I was thrilled that they came in short, regular, and long lengths. They’re still just the tiniest bit long, so I flip the elastic on each ankle under to shorten the legs. You can’t tell a thing!

Set Active Staple SET Uniform Layered Crewneck

Set Active Staple Straight Leg Sweatpants

This vintage-inspired sweatsuit from Set Active is made from 100% cotton, for those who want to prioritize more natural fibers. “I love how soft they feel,” Hsieh says. “Sometimes 100% cotton feels stiff to me, and I’ve found that cotton sweats in particular lay weirdly at the chest when they’re oversized, but these maintain their plushy softness.”

This set is mid-weight, cozy, and warm. “I love a crewneck and sweatpants to sleep in, but sometimes find other sweats to be too much underneath my many layers of comforter and other blankets. This set comes in tons of bold colorways, with contrasting collars and retro logos on the crewneck—so it’s great for anybody who's into the vintage activewear look. The only con? Hsieh, who is 5’3, found that pants run slightly long.

lululemon Scuba Oversized Full-Zip Hoodie

This lululemon hoodie was named the best zip-up in our guide to the best hoodies for its comfy, classic fit. Where the hoodie shines, according to Associate Style & Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz, the pants are just as impressive. Both stand out for the waffle material: A soft, stretchy blend of cotton, modal, and polyester. She finds it more breathable than some of her buttery-smooth cotton sweats. Another perk? “Both pieces are incredibly soft and cozy,” Zitz says. “I love the slightly oversized, waist-length fit of the top. It pairs really well with the matching sweatpants, which are equally comfy and have a flattering drape with a straight-leg fit.”

This set styled with a plain white tee underneath and a pair of comfortable sneakers “happens to be my travel fit of choice,” she says. “The hoodie keeps me warm and cozy during cold flights and early morning departure days, but I can easily unzip it or tie it around my waist if I get too warm.”

The Restore hoodie is one of Vuori’s best sellers, and for good reason. “I love the material,” Richey says. “It’s very soft and feels super durable.” The French terry material (a cotton blend that’s smooth on the outside with brushed fleece on the inside)is made of breathable cotton and sturdy polyester.

As far as sweat sets go, this one has a lot of heft. The Restore line is thicker and denser than the label's BlissBlend or DreamKnit lines, making this set incredibly warm with a high-quality, structured feel. “The softness seems to also stay wash after wash, which is a huge win!” Richey adds.

When it comes to fit, the hoodie has a perfectly oversized shape, but you might benefit from sizing up in the bottoms, particularly if you’re thicker-thighed, Ritchey says. The pant comes in short, regular, and long lengths, giving you even more options to find the right fit.

This Spanx set stands out as a lighter-weight and more polished option. “This set feels so light and airy,” says Zitz. Spanx’s Air Essentials is made of their signature Spacer Fabric (a blend of modal, polyester, and elastane), for an ultra-smooth feel with plenty of stretch.

“It’s one of the most comfortable lounge sets I own, but also one of the nicest looking,” Zitz says. The structured half-zip top and tailored (yet roomy) wide-leg pant have an almost dressed-up look, so you can wear the set to lounge or out of the house. It also comes in nearly 20 colors—a range of neutrals to bright options like red, blue, and plum.

There is one downside: Neither the top nor bottom has pockets. While they might take away from the streamlined look, being able to slip your phone or wallet into a small pocket would be a bonus.

Gap VintageSoft Oversized Henley Pullover

Gap VintageSoft Baggy Wide-Leg Sweatpants

Gap certainly holds its own in the loungewear category. Aside from the cozy feel (thanks to a blend of cotton and polyester), it really shines when it comes to style.

“I love a wide-leg sweatpant,” Zitz says. “I find they look less loungey than a jogger, and this pair is roomy without swallowing up my entire frame.” Even better is the henley top: The button-up design and mock neck make this top look more chic than your average crewneck or half-zip. “It’s unlike any other sweatshirt I own in terms of style,” Zitz says.

One area for improvement: The color options. Our tester opted for a soft blue color, but would have preferred a more neutral gray—it just wasn’t in stock due to the limited colorways.

Rhone is another label that the WH fitness and style editors love. I have personally been a fan of their DreamGlow line for a while. It’s warm, but also has a sleek feel to it. There’s no heaviness to this set at all.

Made primarily of polyester and a small amount of elastane, the fabric also contains lyocell, a semi-synthetic fiber that helps to wick moisture away from the body, creating a slightly cooling effect. This set is ideal for anyone who runs hot or for transitional spring or fall weather. I like to wear it around my apartment on work-from-home days or as a travel outfit.

This is also the set for someone who is a little sweatsuit-reluctant. The top has a slightly cropped and boxy fit, while the pants are a barrel-leg shape (a.k.a. a flared mid-leg and tapered ankle). Combined with the ultra-smooth material, this set looks less frumpy than your old-school sweat suits.

#4788. Bitcoin ETFs near $5B in record monthly outflows amid AI stock rout

US spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded $4.94 billion in November net outflows, exceeding the previous monthly record of $4.51 billion set in June.

US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are approaching $5 billion in monthly net outflows for the first time since their launch in January 2024.

The funds recorded $231.6 million in net outflows on Tuesday, extending their withdrawal streak to six consecutive trading days, according to SoSoValue. November outflows reached $4.94 billion, surpassing the previous monthly record of $4.51 billion in June.

The latest withdrawals bring net outflows for 2026 to about $4.57 billion, erasing the recovery that saw the funds attract $6.34 billion in the third quarter.

Digital asset investment company Teroxx identified rising interest rates and weakness in AI stocks among the factors behind declining ETF demand in its November research report, noting that markets increasingly expect another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

US spot Bitcoin ETF net flows in billions of dollars, with November data through Nov. 20. Source: Teroxx

“In the near term, flows into Bitcoin will remain under pressure as long as artificial intelligence stocks are searching for a bottom and the December Fed decision looms,” Teroxx digital asset researcher Leonardo Larieira said in comments shared with Cointelegraph.

Larieira said a sustained recovery in Bitcoin ETF inflows would require long-term US Treasury yields to stabilize. “Once that happens, returning institutional capital will meet a regulated infrastructure that is far deeper than it was in August,” he added.

#4787. 15 Best Places to Buy Bedding, Editor Picks (2026)

Sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use. Every retailer here comes recommended by an AD editor or contributor who has lived with the bedding at home for a long stretch: flannel kept on the bed through May, linen hauled to a communal laundromat and back, or a sheet set that survives a dog digging in every night.

Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand. Rest assured: they’re all comfy.

For bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop. Its European Linen Sheet Set earned our pick for the best affordable linen sheets, and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker has recently added the brand to her list of favorites. “The price point is unbeatable, and I love that they offer bedding sets in beautiful colorways and a variety of fabric options,” she says. “The quality is also impressive, especially considering the affordability.”

Made from 100% European flax, the sheets cost a fraction of what competitors charge, thanks in part to Quince’s direct-to-consumer model which skips traditional retail markups. “I love its airy nature along with the gorgeous Bordeaux color that complements the rest of my decor,” says Baker. The bedding range extends to quilts and coverlets, , and the brand’s down comforter also made our ranking of the best comforters.

Anyone who has paused a Nancy Meyers movie to study the bedroom should start with Serena & Lily. The brand is based in Sausalito, California, but its textured, breezy bedding and decor would look right at home on any coast, Nantucket included. The range covers lightweight linen and crisp cotton percale in pale colors and easygoing prints.

Of all the bedding Baker has tested, the Nantucket Stripe Sheet Set ranks near the top for its light weight and “worn-in texture,” which keeps the linen soft instead of scratchy. The ruffle trim keeps her bed from looking too plain. “The striped mink print does give a seaside vibe, but it’s been neutral enough to layer with any color bed cover without clashing with the rest of my minimal, romantic decor over the few months I’ve tested the set,” she adds. For a top layer, there’s the scalloped Baywood Quilt, which Alpert likes as a light blanket for “when you want to throw something over while you read your favorite Emily Henry book in bed.”

Boll & Branch sheets arrive feeling as if they’ve already been through several wash cycles, without the fraying or pilling that usually comes with that. Contributor Rachel Fletcher tested the brand’s percale, Supima cotton, flannel, and linen, but its signature sateen stood out most for its long-staple cotton and a soft, smooth finish. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, make them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” she says. Converts can outfit the rest of the room too, with Boll & Branch’s mattresses and bedroom furniture.

Brooklinen started out selling two things, cotton percale and sateen sheets, and has since added cashmere, brushed flannel, and a long list of prints. Pieces come in bundled sets or one at a time, and prices land between the budget brands and the luxury labels. Our editors keep coming back to the linen sheets, which they use in every season.

“Since I don’t live my life on a Greek island, I thought white linen sheets year-round might be a slightly bold move, but the nature of the fiber is versatile and temperature regulating,” says AD contributor Madeleine Luckel, who tested the Core Sheet Set. Fletcher sleeps on the Luxe Sheet Set and credits it with keeping her cool. “I’m a hot sleeper with sensitive skin, and they’re really cool on my skin at night, which is a huge relief,” she says. “I love the breathability of these sheets.”

Few bedding brands have tied their name to sustainability as closely as Coyuchi. Its linen sheets are made from certified organic French flax grown without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, and the brand also offers percale, sateen, and flannel sheets. The earthy color palette is a selling point on its own.

“I love the color, which is what drew me to these sheets in the first place,” says Sam Cochran, global features editor. “They’re the perfect brown—a tad auburn, ever so slightly timeworn in palette.”

Shopping writer Julia Harrison and contributor Kate McGregor agree: Garnet Hill is their “secret spot” for bedding. Harrison is devoted to the flannel sheets and admits she leaves them on the bed through May because “they’re so soft, I’d rather suffer in my own sweat than switch them out.” The ticking stripe is “perfectly classic—like a true vintage piece, but not actually vintage…that might be tough sell in the bedding department.” Alpert also loves her flannel pick, a duvet cover that “signals a cottagecore moment without going over the top.” Paired with her Ostermoor duvet insert, it’s “like climbing under a layer of meringue.” Garnet Hill specializes in vintage-inspired designs, patchwork quilts especially, made in 100% linen and 100% cotton options at reasonable prices.

Cozy Earth makes breathable bedding for people who run hot at night, and its signature bamboo bedding, made of 100% viscose, are the brand’s best-known example. “I honestly thought these sheets were silk,” says contributor Megan Wahn. “That’s how smooth and soft they feel.” Wahn tested them mostly in winter, and despite feeling cool to the touch, they kept her warm. “I’m especially eager to see how they perform in the summer,” she adds. “Something about their smoothness makes me think the summer-night sweats won’t stand a chance.”

Parachute is where we send anyone after classic, well-made cotton bedding. Its sets and bundles are designed with sustainability in mind, and the percale and brushed cotton are made by artisans at the brand’s factory in Portugal.

“We love [Parachute] because the bedding is designed to provide a hotel-like experience, offering a perfect balance of softness and crispness,” says Stephanie Kraus of Stephanie Kraus Designs, whose clients favor the brand’s linen bedding sets. “They become softer with each wash while maintaining their durability and are super soft to sleep in every night.”

Fletcher also praises the brand’s commitment to organic, ethically sourced materials; the Organic Cloud Cotton Duvet Set, for one, is made of Oeko-Tex-certified 100% cotton. “I try a lot of bedding in this line of work and the more I do, the more I appreciate ethical and organic production, even if the price tag is a little higher,” she says.

GreenRow makes charming, long-lasting bedding from recycled and sustainably sourced materials, and it has won over several people on the Shop AD team. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls the Helena Floral Sheet Set “without a doubt, the softest sheets I own.” She compares the cotton satin to velvet, and the butter-yellow florals and green micro-gingham ruffle make the set prettier still. McGregor, meanwhile, is partial to the reversible patchwork quilt. “It’s the kind of blanket that feels substantial without trapping heat or feeling stuffy,” she notes. “I feel cocooned without a down comforter, but I’m not smothered when I sleep sans AC in the warmer months. It’s a year-round bedding piece for me, especially since the color palette can lean moodier or more cheerful depending on my sheet selection.”

Rebecca Udall is a newer name and one worth knowing. Her namesake bedding line is built on romantic, careful details, such as soft-colored decorative embroidery along the sheets. McGregor’s current favorite is this scalloped percale sheet set. “The feel is like a washed percale, crisp but forgiving, and I find that the subtle color on the detailed edge gives the perfect amount of visual interest to my all-white bedscape,” she says. If you want less ornament, try the Georgiana duvet cover, with faint ladderstitch detailing hand-embroidered by artisans in Northern Italy.

Hommey, an Australian brand founded in 2020, first caught on with its boldly striped robes and nightwear. It has since carried those designs into cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers. Across both fabrics, there are more than two dozen colors and prints to choose from. For maximalists who want to try color-blocking, the brand’s bolder colorways are a great place to start.

Baker tested the brown sugar linen duvet cover and found the stonewashed, Oeko-Tex certified flax smoother and more broken-in straight out of the package than the Quince version she already owned (above). “I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes,” Baker says. She pairs the chocolatey shade with burgundy linen sheets for a moodier bed, though it also works as a neutral with lighter sheets in oatmeal, which pick up the cream trim. The one drawback is that the cover has no interior ties, so the insert can shift around inside.

Australian brand Cultiver makes linen sheets and duvets with an easy, beachy look. Its Oeko-Tex certified pieces are an investment, and a worthwhile one. Coverlets are generously sized so they drape loosely, and the envelope-back pillow cases hold their shape without looking stiff. Fletcher has put her set through heavy use and many wash cycles. “Linen is my bedding fabric of choice pretty much 365 days a year, and Cultiver’s high-quality sheet sets do it for me in a way no other brand has. Out of all the sets I’ve tried, this one has stood the test of many washes, my dog digging in them to get cozy at night, and surviving across seasons without feeling worn or threadbare,” she says.

Erica Tanov’s bedding is handmade by artisans in Jaipur, in 100% linen with embroidery drawn from traditional Indian textiles. Harrison calls hers “a lifetime set” that “draws more compliments than anything else in my apartment.” The linen is soft and tough: She hauls this sheet set to her neighborhood laundromat, and it survives the communal machines without damage. It’s the first linen set she’s found to be “city-friendly,” as she calls it. She hasn’t tried the quilts or throw blankets yet, though one already tops her birthday wishlist (this one).

It depends mostly on how you like your bed to feel and how reliable your thermostat is. If you like the crisp coolness of hotel sheets, try percale. If you like a soft, organic feel, try linen for a breezy texture, or bamboo sheets for something similar to silk. Cotton sheets (like Supima sets) are often the most durable over time, especially after many, many washes. Your warmest options are generally flannel sets, and your coolest are generally bamboo and percale. For a basic setup, we recommend a full sheet set (flat sheet included, people) plus a duvet insert with a cover. The cover protects the insert and keeps it clean, so you’ll generally only need to wash the insert every six months rather than weekly like your sheets. Harrison likes to go one step further with a bed blanket underneath her duvet and above her sheets for a bit of weight and additional warmth. If a fluffy duvet isn’t your thing, a quilt or coverlet can take its place and add a little more weight.

Start with the fiber content on the label. Search for 100% cotton, linen (the more organic, the better), and steer clear of polyesters or more plastic fibers, as they’re likely to pill more quickly and break apart in the washer and dryer.

#4786. Hong Kong launches tokenized debt platform with 24-hour settlement

The HKMA’s new platform supports settlement in multiple currencies and handles debt issuance, interest payments and repayment at maturity.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) launched a platform Wednesday that supports round-the-clock settlement of tokenized debt securities in multiple currencies.

The CMU Digital Asset Platform, developed and operated by CMU OmniClear Limited on behalf of the HKMA, uses cash tokens for payment and connects with conventional payment systems and central bank digital currencies.

Its onchain delivery-versus-payment model ensures that the securities and corresponding payment transfer together, or neither transfer occurs. This means the buyer receives the securities only if the seller receives payment.

The platform also handles issuance, interest payments and repayment at maturity, and supports the tokenization of existing debt securities. The HKMA said it aims to improve settlement efficiency and reduce operational costs.

The launch follows a separate expansion of Hong Kong’s digital payment infrastructure. On Nov. 2, the HKMA upgraded its Project Ensemble pilot to support 24/7 interbank settlement of tokenized deposit transactions using tokenized central bank money.

The pilot phase launched in November 2025 and initially used Hong Kong’s conventional real-time gross settlement system. Its applications have included corporate treasury management and transactions involving tokenized money market funds.
